Case A

A1: The seven-day search covered 7 days before publication to now, with data current as of the search, and returned only the earlier region-based requests. The burst at 19 minutes therefore appears to be the first misuse, assuming the burst itself was misuse. The question asks whether the burst was the first misuse of this key. The search only covers 7 days before publication, so earlier misuse is not excluded beyond that window. Still, the earlier requests came from a stable fingerprint in one cloud region, which is consistent with the legitimate owner. The question is whether any misuse happened before the burst. The search window shows only the baseline requests, and between publication and the burst the search returned only those same earlier requests. But "returned only those" covers the full window to now, and the burst should appear in it. The log shows the search ran and returned results, so the data seems complete enough. I answer Yes: within the seven-day window and the period up to the burst, no other differing requests exist. Though the "Yes" is limited to that window, it is the best-supported answer.

A2: The check scored 30 minutes after publication, and the burst at 19 minutes plus the link record (effective before publication) were both available. The record shows the shared destination link existed before publication. The burst happened 11 minutes before scoring. We don't know what inputs the check used, so we can't tell whether it missed evidence available to it. Cannot tell.

A3: A shared payout destination does not by itself show one owner. No, not by itself.

A4: Zero reports at 30 days is weak evidence at best, because absence of reports does not show legitimacy, and no one may have looked. The options are "Yes, weakly", "No", and "Cannot tell". Zero reports is consistent with both outcomes, and reporting may be slow or absent. I choose Cannot tell, as the records give no information on whether reports would have been expected.

A5: Yes. A different fingerprint through a residential proxy, a new webhook, a payout change and a faster schedule right after the key was published warrant investigation.

Case B

B1: D has 0 chargebacks recorded at the account, but the dispute records show 2 chargebacks at account X that dispute payments that are transactions of D. So D's chargebacks may have been misattributed to X, and D's rate is not clearly lower. Cannot tell is plausible, but D's true count may be 2, the same as the others. The records show the disputes are against D's payments, so D's rate is not lower on that basis. I answer No.

B2: The combined measure of 5 percent is an average, so one account could be above 5 percent. No.

B3: The search covered 3 account sources, and we don't know whether that covers all merchant accounts. Cannot tell.

B4: The notes were written by different analysts on different days, but there is no information on whether the second analyst saw the first note or used the same underlying evidence. Cannot tell.

B5: The blocked payment never had a chance to be disputed, so lack of a chargeback does not make it non-fraud. No.

B6: Shared templates and descriptor patterns, plus a person linked to A, justify investigating together. Yes.

RESULT CN-056 | A1: Yes | A2: Cannot tell | A3: No, not by itself | A4: Cannot tell | A5: Yes | B1: No | B2: No | B3: Cannot tell | B4: Cannot tell | B5: No | B6: Yes
